description: Question: does one law of motion fix the orbit of every planet we know? Idea: Kepler's third law, from Newton's gravity, P² = 4π²a³/(G(M★ + m)); in years, astronomical units and solar masses it is P² = a³/M★. The NASA Exoplanet Archive's composite table (pscomppars, one row per planet with the best values) gives the period P, the semi-major axis a and the star's mass for about 5,600 planets. Polars fits log P on log a (slope 1.466 ± 0.002, not 1.5: heavier stars hold wider planets, so the raw fit mixes stars) and log P² on log(a³/M★): slope 0.9985 ± 0.0005 across nearly 10 decades of period (2 hours to a million years), and the star's mass can be read off any one orbit as M = a³/P². Forensic twist: about 55% of the planets agree to better than 1%, because the archive's a for transiting planets is usually computed from P and M★ with this very law; the other half scatter by about ±18% (0.071 dex standard deviation), the disagreement between the papers the period, the orbit and the stellar mass come from. Caveats: the planet's mass is neglected (Jupiter is 0.1% of the Sun); a composite row mixes references; imaging and microlensing semi-major axes are projected separations or model-based. Next: the ps table's per-paper rows (one solution per reference) to see which stellar models disagree; the transit stellar density (a/R★)³/P².
name: Kepler's third law in 5,600 exoplanets
